newsitem.title: UK: British doctor offers test-tube sex selection.
newsitem.headline: British doctor offers test-tube sex selection.

text.p: A British doctor triggered a new genetic furore on Wednesday by announcing he was setting up a test tube sex-selection clinic outside the country.

The announcement from Dr Paul Rainsbury came hot on the heels of a worldwide controversy set off by the cloning of a sheep by scientists in Scotland and speculation the operation could work with humans.
Rainsbury, a consultant medical director of Roding Hospital in a suburb of London, said he was establishing his laboratory in Riyadh and would carry out treatment in Naples, Italy.
He said in a statement he felt he was offering a useful service, even if it was illegal in Britain.
"Those of us who work in the field of human reproduction are accustomed to censure, usually by people who have no idea of the huge distress caused by infertility and childlessness," he said.

"My hope is that any criticism will disappear as people come to understand why we have decided to use existing medical science to help those who face intense personal pressure to produce babies of a specific sex."
Rainsbury said he expected 80 percent of his mostly Asian clients to seek boys.
"Offering sex selection as part of infertility treatment was always going to come. It was simply a question of who was going to be first to grasp the nettle."
For some people, already grappling with the implications of the cloning for the first time of an adult animal, a sheep called Dolly, it was unwelcome news.

"I think things have gone too far already as far as the development of technology is concerned," said Udo Shuklenk, a bioethicist at the University of Central Lancashire's Centre for Professional Ethics.

Rainsbury proposes using existing in-vitro fertilisation (IVF or test-tube) techniques. It is easy to tell what sex a baby will be -- and he promises to implant only embryos of the desired sex in the mother's womb.

Lord Robert Winston of London's Hammersmith Hospital, a pioneer in IVF technology and one of the few experts who legally practice sex-selection, said it was still a dangerous and experimental technique.
"It is a technique which should be used only to overcome the inheritance of sex-linked diseases and not for social reasons," he said.

It is now only legally used in Britain to help couples who might have a baby with a sex-linked disorder such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a wasting disorder affecting only boys, or haemophilia, which also afflicts boys.
"We find this abhorrent as it is increasingly turning children into a commodity," the anti-abortion group Life said.
"It is ethically wrong to say that one sex is more desirable than the other," agreed Dr Vivian Nathanson, the British Medical Association's head of ethics.
BUPA, the private British health insurance company that owns Roding Hospital, disassociated itself from Rainsbury's work.
"This work is completely independent," spokesman Peter Fermoy said. "He neither is researching or practicing this gender selection technique at BUPA Roding Hospital."

Shuklenk pointed out that sex-selection is nothing new. Baby girls are often aborted or left to die in China and India, where boys are highly valued. In China the practice has skewed measurably the ratio of men to women.
"We should look very carefully at biotechnology and decide for each case whether it's a good thing or a bad thing."
